how.title: Four steps, and you can watch every one of them
how.body: There is no step where it decides something you cannot see afterwards. Every reply keeps the article it came from, and every handover keeps its reason.

pricing.title: You pay when the customer stops writing

card.title: Still have questions?
card.text: You’re in good hands from here.

items.q: What if it answers something wrong?
items.a: Every reply keeps the help centre article it was written from, so a wrong answer is traceable in one click rather than a mystery. When it cannot source something it does not improvise — the conversation goes to a person with the context gathered and a draft written. For the first two weeks nothing sends without you.

items.q: Will customers know they are talking to an agent?
items.a: Yes. It introduces itself as an agent, in wording you approve, and it never pretends to be a named person on your team. Asking for a human is enough to move the conversation across, with the full history attached.

items.q: Are we buying this to cut our support team?
items.a: Not from us. The teams running Mitce kept their headcount — what dropped was overtime, weekend cover and the Monday backlog. It takes the order-status half so your people get the half that needs judgement. If the business case is redundancies, we are the wrong vendor.

items.q: Our help centre is a mess. Is that a dealbreaker?
items.a: No, and it is usually the reason to start. It only answers what it can source from your articles, so a thin help centre means fewer automatic replies, never invented ones. The weekly gap report lists the questions that had no article behind them — a to-do list in the order your customers actually ask.

items.q: What happens with an angry customer?
items.a: Sorting reads urgency and tone, so anything that reads as upset moves up the queue instead of waiting behind order-status questions. Those conversations go to a person with the history and a draft ready, not to a cheerful template. Your team keeps the hard ones; that is the point.

items.q: What does week one look like?
items.a: Day one is connecting the inbox and syncing the help centre. After that it runs in shadow: it drafts, you read and sign, and nothing reaches a customer without you. The replies you sign are what it learns your tone from, and at the end of the two weeks you switch on sending for the categories you trust.
